name: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
aliases: candidiasis of skin nails and mucosae

reference.source: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders / IUIS classification of inborn errors of immunity
clinicalPearls: Describes persistent or recurrent infection of the skin, nails and mucous membranes with Candida, typically without invasive dissemination in isolated forms
It is a phenotype rather than a single disease and reflects a defect in the interleukin-17-dependent T-helper-17 pathway that governs mucosal antifungal defence
Recognised monogenic causes include gain-of-function variants in STAT1, defects in the IL-17 axis (IL17RA, IL17F, IL17RC, ACT1), CARD9 deficiency and RORgammaT deficiency
It is a cardinal feature of APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy) due to AIRE deficiency, where it accompanies autoimmune endocrinopathy
CARD9 deficiency is distinctive because it can allow deep-seated and central nervous system fungal invasion rather than purely superficial disease
Associated features vary by genotype and may include autoimmunity, endocrinopathy, aneurysms and, with chronic mucosal inflammation, a raised risk of squamous cell carcinoma
Diagnostic workup should look beyond confirming Candida to define the underlying immunological and genetic mechanism
Management combines antifungal therapy with treatment directed at the underlying defect, such as a JAK inhibitor in STAT1 gain-of-function disease
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis arises from impaired T-helper-17 immunity, the arm of adaptive defence that produces interleukin-17 and interleukin-22 to recruit neutrophils and maintain antifungal barrier function at skin and mucosal surfaces. Different genetic lesions converge on this pathway: STAT1 gain-of-function suppresses T-helper-17 differentiation, defects in interleukin-17 or its receptor block downstream signalling, AIRE deficiency generates neutralising autoantibodies against interleukin-17 cytokines, and CARD9 deficiency impairs the innate sensing of fungi. The shared consequence is inadequate mucosal control of Candida, producing persistent superficial infection, while the specific genotype determines the accompanying autoimmune, endocrine, vascular or invasive features.
additionalDifferentials: CARD9 deficiency with invasive fungal disease
Acquired immunosuppression, diabetes or endocrinopathy predisposing to candidiasis
additionalInvestigations: STAT1 phosphorylation assay and STAT1 gene sequencing
Screening for autoantibodies against interleukin-17 cytokines and for AIRE variants when APECED is suspected
Serum immunoglobulins and endocrine autoantibody and hormone screen
Targeted or panel gene sequencing covering IL17RA, IL17F, ACT1, CARD9 and RORgammaT
Mycological confirmation and assessment for invasive or deep fungal disease where indicated
redFlags: Neurological signs suggesting central nervous system fungal invasion, particularly in CARD9 deficiency
New oral or oesophageal lesion raising concern for squamous cell carcinoma
Features of autoimmune endocrine crisis such as adrenal insufficiency in APECED
Evidence of invasive or disseminated fungal infection
Vascular symptoms in genotypes associated with aneurysm
reference.prognosis: Isolated chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is often chronic but manageable with antifungal therapy, whereas outcome in syndromic forms depends on the associated autoimmune, endocrine, vascular or invasive complications and the response to genotype-directed treatment.
pitfalls: Treating the candidiasis symptomatically without investigating the underlying inborn error
Failing to screen for the autoimmune endocrinopathy of APECED
Underestimating the risk of invasive and CNS fungal disease in CARD9 deficiency
Overlooking the long-term squamous malignancy risk in chronically inflamed mucosa
Assuming a single mechanism when the phenotype has several distinct genetic causes
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
